To make sure your freelance earnings don't trigger a surprise tax bill or penalty next April, here is a practical game plan tailored to your setup.

### 1. Set aside 30% to 35% in a tax reserve
Freelance income has no automatic tax withholding and faces two separate federal taxes:
- **Self-employment (SE) tax (15.3%)**: Covers both the employee and employer shares of Social Security (12.4%) and Medicare (2.9%) on 92.35% of your net business earnings.
- **Federal income tax (22% to 24%)**: Freelance profit stacks on top of your Microsoft W-2 salary and RSU income, landing in your marginal federal bracket. Because Washington has no personal income tax, you only need to cover federal obligations.

For your **$1,200** consulting payment, transfer **$360 to $420** from your Chase checking account into your Ally Online Savings account so it earns interest while staying protected until tax time.

### 2. Track business expenses to lower your taxable net profit
Unlike W-2 wages, you only pay tax on your **net profit** (revenue minus eligible business expenses) reported on Schedule C. Legitimate write-offs directly reduce both income tax and self-employment tax:
- Software subscriptions and design tools (e.g., Figma licenses, font subscriptions, cloud storage)
- Hardware, accessories, and home office equipment purchased specifically for freelance work
- Client-related travel, professional memberships, or invoicing fees

Keep digital receipts and tag these transactions so you have an audit trail when filing.

### 3. Handle payments: W-4 adjustment vs. quarterly estimated taxes
The IRS operates on a pay-as-you-go system. You generally must pay throughout the year if you expect to owe $1,000 or more in unpaid tax at filing time, unless your W-2 withholding satisfies the safe harbor rule (covering 100% of your prior year's tax liability, or 110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000).

You have two easy ways to handle this:
- **Option A (Simplest): Add extra withholding on your Microsoft W-4.** You can enter an extra withholding amount on line 4(c) of your W-4 through payroll. The IRS treats W-2 withholding as if it were paid evenly throughout the entire tax year, avoiding estimated payment vouchers completely.
- **Option B: Make a quarterly payment via IRS Direct Pay.** For income received in April and May (Q2), the quarterly estimated deadline is **June 15**. You can make a quick guest payment online using Form 1040-ES.

If this consulting work is an ongoing project or you expect more invoices this year, let me know roughly how much you anticipate making and we can fine-tune the exact withholding target.
